title: The Decision to Drop the Bomb
objective: After this level you can weigh the arguments historians make about why the US used atomic bombs on Japan in 1945.
summary: Traditionalists, after Stimson (1947), say the bombs saved lives by avoiding an invasion; revisionists, after Alperovitz (1965), point to the Soviets; many stand between.

cards.headline: Within days of two atomic bombs in 1945, World War II was over. Why use them?
cards.body: Historians agree on what happened that August. They still argue about why it happened.

cards.headline: August 1945
cards.body: On August 6, 1945, the United States dropped an atomic bomb on Hiroshima. On August 9 a second fell on Nagasaki. Estimates of deaths in Hiroshima by the end of 1945 range from 90,000 to 166,000. Japan surrendered within days of the Nagasaki bombing. These facts are not in dispute. The reasons are.

cards.headline: The traditional case
cards.body: The first defense came from inside. In a 1947 Harper’s Magazine article, former Secretary of War Henry Stimson pointed to Japan’s refusal to surrender and the cost of an invasion. Historians called traditionalists agree: the bombs were necessary to save American lives and prevent an invasion of Japan.

cards.headline: The revisionist case
cards.body: In 1965 historian Gar Alperovitz argued the opposite. Japan, he said, was already close to surrender, so the bombs weren’t needed; they were meant mainly to strengthen the American hand against the Soviet Union. Revisionists point to a real clue: some US policymakers did hope the bomb’s power might push the Soviets to make concessions.

cards.headline: Between the poles
cards.body: Many historians take positions between the two camps. J. Samuel Walker, criticizing both, concluded that the main motive was to end the war as quickly as possible. Notice how the argument works: both sides accept the same dates and deaths. They disagree about how close Japan was to surrender and what the decision-makers had in mind.

mascot.line: You don’t have to pick a camp today. Practice naming the evidence each side must explain.

cards.headline: The Decision to Drop the Bomb: explained
learned: The US bombed Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945
Traditionalists: the bombs saved lives by avoiding invasion
Revisionists: Japan was near surrender; the target was Moscow
Many historians, like Walker, stand in between

questions.prompt: Which historian argued in 1965 that the atomic bombs were meant mainly to strengthen the US hand against the Soviet Union?

options.label: J. Samuel Walker
options.rationale: Walker concluded the main motive was to end the war quickly.

questions.explanation: Gar Alperovitz argued in 1965 that the bombs were not needed and were aimed at the Soviet Union.

questions.prompt: Which question most divides traditionalists from revisionists?

options.label: Which cities the bombs struck
options.rationale: Both sides agree on Hiroshima and Nagasaki.

options.label: How close Japan already was to surrender
Whether the bombs were dropped at all
options.rationale: No one disputes that they were dropped.

options.label: In which year the war ended
options.rationale: Both sides agree the war ended in 1945.

questions.explanation: Traditionalists say an invasion was the alternative; revisionists say Japan was already close to surrender, so the bombs served other aims.

questions.prompt: Stimson defended the bombs as a way to end a war sooner. Which Civil War campaign from Level 56 also aimed to wreck an enemy’s ability to keep fighting?

options.label: Burgoyne’s march to Saratoga
options.rationale: That was a British army in the Revolution (Level 26).

options.label: The Fort Monroe escapes
options.rationale: Those were escapes to Union lines, not a campaign.

options.label: Sherman’s march from Atlanta to Savannah
The New York draft riots
options.rationale: Those were riots on the home front, not a campaign.

questions.explanation: Sherman aimed to wreck the Confederacy’s ability to make war and bring the war home to Southern civilians.
